name: onesie
description: Use when a script needs a onesie judgment on one piece of text, as a probability, one of several named options or a rubric level, and before prompting a general model and parsing its reply. Covers --ask, --pick, --rate, --desc, question files and free dry runs. For a file of many records, also load onesie-stream.
compatibility: Requires the onesie binary on PATH. A key is needed for anything but --print-request and --print-questions.

rules.short: Ask every question you might need in one call.
rules.why: Questions in one request are evaluated in parallel against the same state, so adding a question barely moves latency. A thirteen question briefing measured about 9 times cheaper and about 13 times faster in one call than in thirteen separate ones. Ask everything you might want and ignore the answers you do not use. A second call is justified only when the first answer decides what the next state or option set contains.
rules.bad: for q in 'is this urgent' 'do they want money back' 'is the writer angry'; do onesie "$q" --state "$t"; done
rules.good: onesie --ask urgent='is this urgent' --ask refund='do they want money back' --ask angry='is the writer angry' --state 'The customer wants a refund and says the shipment never arrived.' -o values

rules.short: Put each shape or policy flag right after the --ask it belongs to.
rules.why: Nothing warns when you meant a flag for every question. With two asks and a trailing `--threshold`, `--print-questions` shows the threshold attached only to the second question and the first left with none.
rules.bad: onesie --ask urgent='is this urgent' --ask refund='do they want money back' --threshold 0.5 --print-questions
rules.good: onesie --ask urgent='is this urgent' --threshold 0.5 --ask refund='do they want money back' --threshold 0.5 --print-questions

rules.short: Ask yes or no as a plain question, one of N with --pick, a degree with --rate.
rules.why: A bare question returns `value`, a probability from 0 to 1, and no confidence, because one number describes a two outcome distribution fully. `--pick` returns `value`, the winning name, with `confidence` and `p`, the probability of each option. `--rate` returns `value`, the most likely level, with `score`, where 0 is the lowest level, `norm`, the score scaled to run from 0 to 1, `confidence` and `p`. A policy flag adds `decision` and `fallback`, covered in the onesie-gate skill, and `-o values` then prints the decision in place of the value. Options split on the comma exactly, so `--pick 'a, b'` names the second option ` b` with its space. When a name holds a comma, set another separator first, as in `--sep '|' --pick 'yes, refund|no, keep'`.
rules.bad: onesie 'which team owns this, billing, shipping or support' --state 'my package never arrived'
rules.good: onesie --ask team='which team owns this' --pick billing,shipping,support --state 'my package never arrived'

rules.short: Use --rate, not a yes or no probability, to measure how much.
rules.why: Asking whether a candidate is strong in Python measured 0.32 for two years of professional experience and 0.76 for eight. 0.32 means the model doubts the claim, not that the candidate is a third of the way to expert. There is no cutoff that maps either number onto a level, so use `--rate` when you want degree.
rules.bad: onesie 'is the candidate strong in Python' --state 'The candidate has two years of professional experience writing Python.'
rules.good: onesie 'how strong is the candidate in Python' --rate none,basic,working,expert --state 'The candidate has two years of professional experience writing Python.'

rules.short: Retune a threshold whenever the shape or the model changes.
rules.why: The gap between shapes is not a fixed offset. Asking whether a report is good measured 0.61 as a bare question against 0.84 for yes under a yes or no choice, and asking whether an essay is well organized measured 0.33 against 0.02, the order reversed. A question and its negation summed to 0.96, 1.04 and 1.20 across three different questions, never landing on exactly 1. Retune any threshold when the shape changes, and log the model from the response, since `jev-latest` moves on release and a tuned threshold drifts with it.

rules.short: Compute the fact in code, then ask about the computed fact.
rules.why: onesie does no arithmetic, reads dates as text and miscounts. It answers the bad example below anyway, with no warning. Compute the age, the count or the comparison first, and pass the computed fact in the state.
rules.bad: onesie 'is this ticket more than 30 days old' --state 'created 2024-01-01'

rules.short: Send the field the question is about, not the whole record.
rules.why: Accuracy drops as unrelated fields pile up in the state, and drops further when the answer means following a reference from one field to another. Pass only the field the question is about. Over a stream, `--map '.ticket.text'` picks that field out of every record, and the onesie-stream skill covers it.
rules.bad: onesie 'is this ticket urgent' -i json --state '{"id":482,"customer":"Jordan Miles","address":"219 Birch Ln","ticket":{"text":"the server is down"}}'
rules.good: onesie 'is this ticket urgent' --state 'the server is down'

rules.short: Say what an option, a level or a yes means with --desc.
rules.why: `--desc KEY=TEXT` binds to the nearest `--ask` like any group flag. The key is an option name for `--pick`, a level label for `--rate`, and `yes` or `no` for a yes or no question. A key the question does not have exits 2 and lists the ones it does. Describe every level of a `--rate` or none of them, since a partial rubric exits 2. A partly described `--pick` only warns. `--ask NAME=@FILE` and `--desc KEY=@FILE` read the text from a file.
rules.good: onesie --ask team='which team owns this' --pick billing,shipping --desc billing='charges, refunds and invoices' --desc shipping='delivery and tracking' --state 'my package never arrived'

rules.short: Keep a question set you reuse in a file written by --print-questions, and load it with -f by path or by name.
rules.why: `--print-questions > q.yaml` writes the questions, their descriptions, their policy flags and any assertion as YAML, and `onesie -f q.yaml` reads it back. Each top level key is a question id holding `ask` and optionally `pick` or `rate`, `yes_means` and `no_means`, `threshold`, `min_confidence` and `fallback`. A top level `assert` or `abstain_if` is the file's gate. An unknown key exits 2 rather than being ignored. An `--ask` beside `-f` adds a question, and reusing an id from the file needs `--replace`. `-f` also takes a request body, a file with a `questions` key such as `--print-request` writes. Save a set the repository shares as `.onesie/questions/NAME.yaml`, after `mkdir -p .onesie/questions` since the redirect creates no directory, or one for every project under `questions` in the config dir `auth set` uses, and `-f NAME` finds it. A value with no slash and no dot that is not a file in the working directory is a name, looked up in the nearest `.onesie/questions` at or above the working directory, then in the config dir, as `NAME.yaml`, `NAME.yml` or `NAME.json`. A name found nowhere, or with two files in one directory, exits 2 and names the directories. `onesie questions` lists every name with the file it resolves to.

rules.short: Use --stats for a run summary and --usage for the tokens of each answer.
rules.why: `--stats` writes one line to stderr at exit, with the requests, failures, skips, tokens, attempts and model, so it never mixes into the answers on stdout. `--usage` adds the API's `usage` object to each json record and to the table header. A 200 whose answers onesie cannot use still spent its tokens, so its json error record carries the `usage` object too. `-o values`, `-r`, `-o raw`, `-o csv` and `-o tsv` have no place for it, and `-q` writes nothing, so they all refuse it with exit 2 before any request.
rules.good: onesie 'is this urgent' --state 'the server is down' --stats --usage -o json

rules.short: Run it once with --print-request before running it for real.
rules.why: `--print-request` and `--print-questions` make no network call and need no key. `--print-request` shows the exact body, the state and the model, but a body carries no policy, so a `--threshold` or `--fallback` does not show there. It checks and then ignores the gate in a `-f` file, so a gated file can be dry run, and it exits 2 on `--assert` or `--abstain-if` typed as a flag. `--print-questions` shows every question with the policy flags that bound to it and the assertion, and reads no state.
rules.good: onesie --ask urgent='is this urgent' --ask team='which team owns this' --pick billing,shipping,support --state 'my package never arrived' --print-request

rules.short: Pick the provider with --provider or ONESIE_PROVIDER, and pin models per provider.
rules.why: typesafe is the default and reads `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`, plus `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` and `TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL` when they are set. openrouter reads `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` alone, and never falls back to the TypeSafe key or those two variables. `jev-latest` works on both, but a pinned model id does not carry over: TypeSafe pins `jev-1.13.0`, OpenRouter pins `typesafe/jev-1.13`. `onesie auth status` names the provider and where its key came from.
rules.good: onesie --provider openrouter 'is this urgent' --state 'the server is down' --print-request
